qualifications: Source-addressed is a code assessment, not a passing regression-suite claim.
No complete checkout, build, typecheck, Vitest, Playwright, pytest, live Hermes, or power-loss suite was executed.
The container Node version is below the repository declared supported minimum; benchmark times are environment-specific.
R means an isolated source-backed mechanism was exercised, not a reproduced full-application incident.

findings.title: The new knowledge move helper can delete a concurrent replacement of its source
findings.trigger: A note or document is moved while an external editor atomically replaces its source file after the destination hard link is created.
findings.mechanism: moveNoReplace performs await fs.link(source, dest), then await fs.unlink(source). The second pathname lookup can name a different inode. Linking preserves the original contents at the destination, but unlinking then removes the newly saved external edit. The note-move plan does not protect this live-operation interval. Document moves share the helper.
findings.impact: The move can report success while the latest source content is lost. This introduces the source-replacement failure previously identified in the workspace into the newly introduced knowledge helper.
findings.fix: Use an atomic no-replace move primitive where supported, with a supported platform implementation. Do not substitute link followed by an unconditional source unlink. If the platform cannot provide the intended guarantee, refuse or expose a non-destructive copy operation. A second stat alone is not an atomic solution.
findings.required_regression_test: Suspend immediately after linking, replace the source using an external rename, and resume. Verify the replacement survives and that the operation does not claim a completed move of the newer file. Exercise both note and document callers.
findings.verification: reproduce.mjs: real temporary files, deterministic external source replacement, selected helper transcribed without changing control flow. Destination retained "original"; source disappeared; "new external edit" was lost.
findings.qualification: This requires a concurrent external writer. It is not a claim that uncontended moves always lose data.

findings.title: The unsupported-hard-link fallback silently restores the destination-overwrite race
findings.trigger: Hard-link creation returns EPERM, ENOSYS, or EOPNOTSUPP, and another process creates the destination after the fallback existence check.
findings.mechanism: The fallback awaits lstat(dest), then invokes ordinary fs.rename(source, dest). On a filesystem with replacing rename semantics, the gap allows a new destination to be overwritten. An error other than absence from lstat is also treated as nonexistence. The helper advertises no-replace behavior but makes it dependent on the filesystem.
findings.impact: A note/document move or a new-note publication can destroy the destination created by another writer. The ordinary hard-link success path fixes the old destination race; the fallback does not.
findings.fix: Keep no-replace semantics mandatory across fallback paths. Use an atomic platform primitive or fail closed with an actionable unsupported-operation error. Distinguish ENOENT from permission and I/O failures.
findings.required_regression_test: Inject an unsupported-hard-link error and create the destination immediately after the absence check. Require a conflict and byte-for-byte preservation of the destination. Repeat with a destination stat permission error.
findings.verification: reproduce.mjs: injected EOPNOTSUPP followed by real filesystem operations reproduced replacement of "external destination" by "incoming".
findings.qualification: The hard-link error is deliberately injected; this was not a survey of network filesystems or operating systems.

findings.title: Document uploads and ZIP imports bypass no-overwrite publication
findings.trigger: An upload/import using a non-replacing conflict policy passes its existence check, then an external process creates the target before publication.
findings.mechanism: The document placement path and the ZIP note branch call vault.atomicWrite without expect. The new no-replace path inside atomicWrite is selected only for expect.hash === null. Without it, publication still uses a replacing rename, even when the earlier upload policy was ask or keep.
findings.impact: A user-selected non-overwriting import can overwrite content created concurrently. The central helper improvement does not protect callers that do not pass the required precondition.
findings.fix: Carry conflict policy and expected target identity into every publication call. New destinations need an atomic absence precondition; explicitly replacing destinations need a version precondition where supported. Share this preparation between single uploads and ZIP imports.
findings.required_regression_test: Use actual upload and ZIP routes with a hook between conflict resolution and publication. Create an external file at the chosen path and verify ask/keep never replaces it. Include both document and Markdown entries.
findings.verification: reproduce.mjs exercised the actual publication branch selected by these callers using real temporary files. It reproduced external content replacement, but did not execute the Fastify routes.

findings.title: A process-recording failure leaves a spawned child running without supervision
findings.trigger: The child process is successfully spawned, but the synchronous onSpawn callback fails, for example because its coding_processes database write fails.
findings.mechanism: spawnCli invokes onSpawn before installing its timers, output handlers, close/error handlers, and returned stop interface. The callback exception unwinds the function. The caller can record preparation failure, but no CliRun handle was returned and the detached child already exists.
findings.impact: The application can show a failed run while executable work continues outside its active process tracking. Recovery may also lack the durable process row needed to find it.
findings.fix: Install supervision and exception handling before invoking fallible bookkeeping. On bookkeeping failure, terminate and reap the complete process group before propagating failure. Prefer durable admission metadata before launch, while still handling the spawn-to-record crash interval explicitly.
findings.required_regression_test: Make onSpawn throw after a harmless long-running test child starts. Require the child/group to be gone, no unhandled events, and a terminal visible outcome. Test the same failure with an actual database-write rejection.
findings.verification: process-reproductions.mjs executed the SHA-verified process module with a harmless Node child. The function threw, the child remained alive, and no stop handle was returned. The test explicitly killed the group afterward.

findings.title: Stop and the wall-clock limit stop supervising a group when its leader exits
findings.trigger: A CLI leader exits while a descendant remains alive, either holding inherited standard I/O open or running with detached/ignored standard I/O.
findings.mechanism: stop returns immediately when child.exitCode or child.signalCode is set. groupGone is performed only after a stop was recorded. With inherited I/O, close and done can remain pending while the timeout and explicit Stop both do nothing. With ignored I/O, done can resolve on a successful leader exit and the caller can forget the process record while a descendant continues.
findings.impact: One variant hangs the run queue and potentially shutdown; the other reports completion while background work remains alive. These are two observable consequences of the same leader-versus-group ownership error, counted once.
findings.fix: Define and supervise the lifetime of the whole owned execution group, not just the leader. Allow Stop to act after leader exit, reconcile surviving descendants before completion, and retain durable ownership while any may remain. Account for process-group identifier reuse and escaped descendants in the platform strategy.
findings.required_regression_test: Test a leader that spawns a harmless worker and exits for both inherited-I/O and ignored-I/O configurations. Require timeout and Stop to terminate the worker and done to settle only according to the documented group policy.
findings.verification: Two checks in process-reproductions.mjs executed the SHA-verified module. An inherited-I/O worker survived both a 150 ms configured wall limit and explicit Stop; another survived successful done resolution. All test groups were cleaned up.

findings.title: A requested coding-run model is recorded but not passed to the CLI
findings.trigger: A room turn selects a model different from the coding agent default, or the default changes between admission and execution.
findings.mechanism: The dispatcher passes job.model. startRun stores req.model ?? agent.model in its intent and run row, but execute receives only the input, admitted agent, and room. Its driver.buildArgs call uses the freshly loaded agent.model rather than the admitted/requested model.
findings.impact: The model actually invoked can differ from the user selection and from the run record. This affects behavior, cost interpretation, and reproducibility.
findings.fix: Carry the effective admitted model through the execution record and into driver arguments. If changing queued runs to a new default is intentional, represent that transition explicitly and keep the run metadata consistent with the launched model.
findings.required_regression_test: Set agent default A, request model B, and inspect both the admitted database row and the fake CLI argv. Both must identify B. Then change the default while the turn is queued.
findings.verification: Source-traced across the dispatcher, runtime, and a driver that honors its supplied model. No real CLI/model invocation was performed.

findings.title: Stop during asynchronous preflight still permits a new child to launch
findings.trigger: A stop request arrives after execute checks stopBeforeStart but while CLI detection, workspace checking, or the running observation is awaited.
findings.mechanism: Those awaits are followed by spawnCli without another cancellation check. The code does check stopBeforeStart afterward, but at that point it sends Stop to a process that has already been launched.
findings.impact: Work can begin after the user has stopped a still-unlaunched queued turn. Immediate signaling is not equivalent to preventing execution; startup code or tools can act before the signal is processed.
findings.fix: Recheck cancellation and shutdown at the final admission boundary immediately before spawning, and between fallback attempts. Do not perform a visible queued-to-running transition for a turn that should never launch.
findings.required_regression_test: Hold CLI detection or the running-observation promise, issue Stop, then resolve the promise. Assert the injected spawn function is never called and the run reaches the appropriate cancelled/interrupted state.
findings.verification: Source-traced asynchronous interleaving. This particular service-level path was not executed.

findings.title: A failed terminal observation is swallowed after the runtime forgets the active run
findings.trigger: A CLI ends, but committing its terminal observation fails because of a transient database/ingestion error or validation failure.
findings.mechanism: finish catches the rejection and reports it only through onError. The surrounding queue can consequently complete and remove the active entry as though terminal persistence succeeded. There is no durable terminal-outcome retry in this path, and the process row may already have been removed.
findings.impact: A finished process can leave its run queued/running and its reply streaming until a separate recovery path intervenes. Subsequent controls lack the original live execution handle.
findings.fix: Separate process termination from durable result delivery. Retain a retryable terminal outcome until ingestion confirms it, with bounded retry/backoff and an explicit degraded state. Do not turn a failed completion commit into silent success.
findings.required_regression_test: Reject the first terminalObservation submission, then recover ingestion. Require the same terminal result to be retried without relaunching the CLI and without leaving a streaming reply behind.
findings.verification: Source-traced failure path, not a database fault-injection integration run.
findings.qualification: This requires a persistence failure; it is not asserted for successful terminal commits.

findings.title: Orchestration preflight can accept coding agents that its executor cannot dispatch
findings.trigger: A request includes a coding agent as an allowed orchestration worker and receives the merged team list used by the HTTP routes.
findings.mechanism: startServer constructs Orchestrator with the raw Hermes port before constructing the coding runtime. buildApp wraps only its own local port variable with withCodingAgents. The routes pass that merged list to preflight/create, which checks identity, readiness, and lifecycle but not dispatch support. The executor retains its raw Hermes startRun boundary.
findings.impact: An API configuration can pass readiness validation and be stored even though subsequent work for that agent reaches the wrong runtime. A UI that filters such agents does not repair the API/executor mismatch.
findings.fix: Choose one supported contract: reject non-Hermes workers consistently at preflight/create, or inject the same capability-aware merged execution port into the executor. Verify stop/recovery as well as start before enabling a runtime.
findings.required_regression_test: Construct the real application wiring with a fake Hermes port and a fake coding runtime. Include a coding worker in preflight and create; require either an explicit unsupported response or dispatch exclusively to the coding fake.
findings.verification: Source-traced object wiring and admission checks. No production orchestration was launched.
findings.qualification: This does not assume coding-agent orchestration is a promised feature. Rejecting unsupported combinations is a valid fix.

findings.title: Valid constructor identifiers are read as inherited object properties
findings.status: new regression and adjacent validation gap
findings.trigger: A workflow contains the allowed identifier constructor as a node without an explicit saved position, or as an omitted optional start input.
findings.mechanism: The schemas permit constructor. Plain-object lookups treat the inherited Object constructor as a present value. moveNode chooses it ahead of the actual drawing position and saves undefined coordinates. validateInputs reads the same inherited function instead of undefined and attempts string operations/iteration.
findings.impact: Moving a different node can make the layout invalid and unsavable. A valid optional input name can make a start request fail with TypeError rather than pass validation. Both are one unsafe map-key assumption, counted together.
findings.fix: Use Map, null-prototype records, or own-property checks at every externally named key lookup. Keep schema and runtime treatment aligned; silently reserving a previously valid name requires compatibility handling.
findings.required_regression_test: Pin a workflow containing constructor by moving a different node and validate the serialized layout. Start a definition with an omitted optional constructor input, then with explicit empty and nonempty values. Add prototype-named cases wherever schemas allow them.
findings.verification: focused-logic-checks.mjs executed the SHA-verified moveNode helper and produced constructor: {} after JSON serialization. A separately transcribed validateInputs body reproduced TypeError for the omitted input. Rendering and HTTP integration were not executed.

findings.title: A later compaction from another browser reopens an already completed busy state
findings.trigger: Browser A starts command A and receives its completion; browser B later completes another compaction for the same session.
findings.mechanism: MeterView retains running = A even after its matching result arrives. It computes busy by comparing that retained ID with only the latest compaction command ID. The reducer later replaces the latest result with B, making A != B and setting busy true again. No code clears A upon matched completion.
findings.impact: Browser A can show Compacting indefinitely after both operations have actually ended, hiding the normal result/control state until the component is reset.
findings.fix: Track completion of the locally pending command and clear pending state when that exact terminal result arrives. Treat later external compactions as independent updates. Provide authoritative command reconciliation after missed events/reset rather than relying on one latest-event slot.
findings.required_regression_test: Mount two session views, complete A, then publish B. Browser A must remain idle and display the newer result appropriately. Also test a result arriving before the POST promise resolves.
findings.verification: Source-traced React state machine; the smaller running/answeredId expression was executed in focused-logic-checks.mjs. No React browser test was run.

findings.title: Snapshot cancellation is not propagated into existing network fetchers
findings.trigger: A snapshot is superseded, times out, or loses its observers while a fetch definition does not consume the supplied AbortSignal.
findings.mechanism: The registry now passes a signal and races the resulting promise against cancellation. The concrete sessionContextQuery fetcher still accepts no signal and calls apiFetch without one. Rejecting the wrapper stops using the result but does not cancel the underlying fetch. Repeated attempts can therefore overlap actual requests despite the registry comment describing one request per entry.
findings.impact: The fix improves logical recovery but does not provide its intended network/work bound for this call site. Slow requests can continue consuming browser and server resources after replacement.
findings.fix: Thread the signal through every StreamQueryDefinition fetcher and its API calls, and audit the remaining definitions for the same omission. Test observable underlying fetch cancellation, not merely rejection of the registry wrapper.
findings.required_regression_test: Use a delayed fetch mock that records signal abortion. Trigger timeout, supersession, idle eviction, and disposal; require the old network call to receive cancellation and no stale result to apply.
findings.verification: The cancellation-versus-underlying-work distinction was exercised in a smaller promise check. The concrete missing signal was confirmed in source; TanStack/network integration was not run.
findings.qualification: The updated buffer limit and follow-up scheduling are genuine improvements. This finding does not claim those old branches remain unchanged.

findings.title: The move-plan path disables Knowledge for a valid linked Git worktree
findings.trigger: The configured vault is a linked Git worktree, whose .git entry is a file pointing to its administrative directory.
findings.mechanism: planFile appends score-move-plan.json beneath root/.git as though .git were always a directory. recoverMove receives ENOTDIR when reading this path. Its catch handles only ENOENT as harmless, then calls clearPlan, which also throws ENOTDIR. Startup recovery consequently fails even when there is no interrupted move.
findings.impact: The application can disable the entire Knowledge capability for a vault that Git itself recognizes as a valid working tree.
findings.fix: Resolve administrative paths through Git, for example git rev-parse --git-path with appropriate path normalization. Do not assume .git is a directory. Gracefully distinguish a missing plan from an unusable plan location.
findings.required_regression_test: Create an actual repository and linked worktree, start Knowledge there, and perform/recover a move. Repeat with a normal repository and with Git unavailable.
findings.verification: reproduce.mjs created a real Git worktree. Git recognized it, while both plan read and forced plan removal failed with ENOTDIR. The full KnowledgeVault class was not booted in this fixture.

findings.title: Deleting a completed backlink rewrite can permanently block move recovery
findings.trigger: A multi-file move is interrupted after some rewrite items are persisted as done. Before recovery, an external editor deletes one of those already completed backlink notes.
findings.mechanism: finishMove skips done items when applying rewrites, but later calls indexFile for every done, non-skipped path. The deleted note yields 404. The plan is not cleared, and recoverMove can fail at the same point on each subsequent startup.
findings.impact: An unrelated external deletion can wedge recovery and, through Knowledge startup failure handling, disable the vault feature. The durable plan creates a retry path but not a convergent one for this case.
findings.fix: Revalidate all recovery items before indexing. Represent deletion or later changes as explicit conflicts, preserve independent external operations, finish the remaining safe work, and surface skipped paths without failing global startup.
findings.required_regression_test: Interrupt after a rewrite is marked done, remove that file externally, and restart twice. Both startups must succeed, the deletion must remain preserved, and the move plan must reach a stable completed/conflicted outcome.
findings.verification: Source-traced deterministic recovery path. A complete database-backed restart test was not executed.

findings.title: Individual stat failures still become false deletion evidence
findings.trigger: Directory enumeration succeeds, but lstat for a previously indexed note/document fails transiently for a reason other than genuine disappearance.
findings.mechanism: The new coverage tracking protects subtrees whose directory read fails. The per-file lstat catch still skips the entry without recording that individual path as unverified. The subsequent removal pass sees an absent, covered path and removes its index entry.
findings.impact: A temporary filesystem or permission error can still remove existing content from search/tree state and emit a deletion event. A later successful scan may repair it, but the false deletion has already been presented.
findings.fix: Propagate coverage/verification status for individual entries as well as directories. Distinguish confirmed ENOENT from EACCES and other I/O failures, retaining prior index state for unverified paths.
findings.required_regression_test: Let readdir return a known file and inject EACCES or EIO into only that file stat. Require no index removal or deleted event. Then restore access and verify normal scanning.
findings.verification: Source-traced scan/removal path. No OS permission fault integration run was performed.

findings.title: Invalidating a document removes it from the index without announcing the change
findings.trigger: An externally edited, previously indexed document becomes oversized, ceases to be a regular supported file, or no longer matches its expected type.
findings.mechanism: ingestExisting removes the existing index row but returns false. scan treats false as no change and does not append the path to changed, so it emits no knowledge.changed event for that removal.
findings.impact: The server index and an already open browser can disagree indefinitely until another invalidation or refresh occurs. Search, the file tree, and counts can show a document no longer present in the authoritative index.
findings.fix: Return an explicit outcome such as unchanged, upserted, removed, or unreadable. Publish removals when state actually changed, while retaining prior state for merely unreadable files.
findings.required_regression_test: Index a valid document, replace it externally with invalid bytes, run scan with announce enabled, and assert both row removal and one coherent notification. Verify that an already invalid unindexed file does not repeatedly emit.
findings.verification: The return-value/notification logic was exercised in a simplified state check; the full document worker and database pipeline were not executed.

findings.title: Rebuilding the disposable index changes a tracked document into an unversioned document
findings.trigger: A document was versioned while at or below 10 MiB, then grew above that threshold while retaining its existing versioned status, and the Knowledge index is rebuilt.
findings.mechanism: ingestExisting preserves versioning with size <= MAX_VERSIONED_BYTES || known.versioned === 1. rebuild deletes the rows that provide known.versioned, and the fresh scan classifies the same large, already Git-tracked file as unversioned. It does not recover the status from Git tracking.
findings.impact: A supposedly disposable-index rebuild alters history availability and subsequent versioning behavior. Existing Git history is not itself erased, but the application no longer consistently treats the document as tracked.
findings.fix: Derive tracking status from Git or persist it outside disposable index state. A rebuild must reconstruct the same semantic state rather than reapply first-upload size policy to established files.
findings.required_regression_test: Version a small document, grow it to 12 MiB while retaining tracking, rebuild, and compare versioned status/history operations before and after. Include restore and deletion behavior.
findings.verification: The before/after versioning predicate was exercised in a smaller logic check. No full 12 MiB document extraction or rebuild integration run was performed.

findings.title: ZIP note imports bypass embedded-image validation used by ordinary saves
findings.trigger: A ZIP contains a text-valid Markdown note with an embedded image that ordinary note saving would reject, such as an unsupported data-image type or an excessive image payload.
findings.mechanism: The ZIP note branch directly calls atomicWrite and indexNote. Its preparation validates the general text/type/size rules, but does not invoke validateNoteImages. Ordinary writeNote does invoke that function.
findings.impact: Import and edit paths disagree about allowed content. A ZIP can create a note that is accepted initially but fails a later ordinary save, or bypasses the documented per-image validation policy.
findings.fix: Centralize note-content preparation and validation, and reuse it for ZIP extraction, single-file uploads, restores where appropriate, and ordinary writes. Keep import-level errors explicit rather than letting one bad entry silently create an uneditable note.
findings.required_regression_test: Compare ordinary upload and ZIP import of identical notes containing invalid base64, unsupported image MIME, mismatched magic bytes, and oversized embedded images. Outcomes should match.
findings.verification: Source-traced validation-path mismatch. No browser exploit or executable-content test was attempted.
findings.qualification: This is not a demonstrated XSS vulnerability. Browser sanitization and rendering boundaries were not shown to fail.

findings.title: The accepted .markdown extension is incompatible with note writing and scanning
findings.trigger: The user uploads or imports a file named chapter.markdown, an extension explicitly recognized as a note.
findings.mechanism: classifyName recognizes md, markdown, and txt, but only converts txt to md. parseNotePath and the filesystem walk recognize only .md. The direct upload therefore reaches a writer that rejects the classified name. The ZIP branch can write/index the file directly, after which ordinary opening or later scans disagree.
findings.impact: A supported-looking upload can fail unexpectedly, or an imported file can become inaccessible/unlisted through the note interface despite remaining on disk.
findings.fix: Normalize .markdown to .md at the same boundary as .txt, with consistent conflict resolution, or deliberately support both extensions across paths, scans, routes, links, and exports.
findings.required_regression_test: Upload and ZIP-import .md, .markdown, .txt, and case variants, then open, scan, rename, export, and restart. Every accepted file must remain discoverable and editable.
findings.verification: The literal classification and path predicates were exercised in focused-logic-checks.mjs. End-to-end upload/import tests were not run.

findings.title: The repaired Markdown parser still rewrites literal code inside lists and blockquotes
findings.trigger: A note contains a fenced code block nested in a list with blank lines, or indented code nested inside a blockquote, and a referenced-looking note name is moved.
findings.mechanism: The custom block parser does not fully model Markdown containers. In the tested examples, it returns no code range for the nested literal text, then parseWikilinks treats [[Target]] as a live link and rewriteLinks replaces it.
findings.impact: Renaming a note changes code examples that should remain literal. Backlink extraction is also incorrect for these cases. Fixes for simple fences and escapes do not cover nested block structure.
findings.fix: Use a container-aware Markdown tokenizer or parse block/container structure before link extraction. Maintain one shared source-range interpretation for indexing, headings, images, and rewrite operations.
findings.required_regression_test: Add the exact list-contained fence and blockquote-indented-code fixtures in links-results.json. Require codeRanges to exclude their literal contents and rewriteLinks to leave the entire input unchanged.
findings.verification: links-reproductions.mjs ran the SHA-verified links module and changed Target to Renamed in both code examples. A separate CommonMark parser confirmed both examples were code blocks.

findings.title: Quadratic array rebuilding makes modest Markdown inputs block the event loop
findings.status: new regression with related pre-existing hot path

sources.symbol: codeRanges byLength buckets; buildNoteIndex suffix buckets

findings.trigger: A note has many short inline-code spans of the same delimiter length, or a large vault has many notes sharing a basename such as README.md.
findings.mechanism: For each backtick run, codeRanges replaces the entire same-length candidate array with [...old, position]. Total copied entries grow quadratically. buildNoteIndex similarly recopies each shared suffix bucket. These synchronous routines are used in indexing and other request/scan paths.
findings.impact: A 128,000-byte inline-code sample took 13,954 ms in the isolated test, despite being far below the note-size limit. It can stall other JavaScript work in the same process. Common-basename indexing has a separate manifestation of the same repeated-copy pattern.
findings.fix: Allocate each bucket once and push in place, then keep subsequent processing linear or n log n. Add input-size/operation-budget tests and move expensive parsing off the main event loop where appropriate. Do not rely only on a multi-megabyte byte cap.
findings.required_regression_test: Benchmark 4k, 8k, 16k, and 32k inline spans and common-basename note sets. Assert a reasonable scaling ratio and bounded latency rather than a hardware-specific exact duration.
findings.verification: Actual SHA-verified code was benchmarked. Inline-code measurements were 39/433/2883/13954 ms for 16/32/64/128 KB. buildNoteIndex was also measured at 4k/8k/16k notes (23/70/524 ms).
findings.qualification: Times are from this container on Node v22.16.0, not a benchmark of the supported production runtime or a live server. The copying complexity is independent of that exact timing.

findings.title: A successful move response does not identify backlink rewrites skipped for conflict
findings.trigger: A backlink note changes externally after the rewrite plan is prepared, so the safe rewrite check correctly detects a conflict.
findings.mechanism: finishMove marks the item skipped and done, logs a warning on the server, and continues. The successful return contains only the destination path and a count of updated notes, not the skipped paths or a partial-completion status.
findings.impact: Content preservation is improved, but a user requesting link updates is not told which links remain broken or need repair. A numeric update count alone does not distinguish no affected links from skipped conflicted links.
findings.fix: Return explicit partial-completion information, including the skipped paths and reasons, and surface it in the move UI. Preserve the conservative refusal to overwrite concurrent edits.
findings.required_regression_test: Cause one of several planned backlink writes to conflict. Require success/partial status to list that exact skipped note while reporting the rewrites that did complete.
findings.verification: Source-traced API result and conflict branch. UI handling of a proposed response shape was not implemented or tested.

findings.title: The bounded media scrub never advances beyond a retained prefix of the store
findings.trigger: The media store contains more than the 256 MiB per-sweep hash budget and its early rows remain retained across sweeps.
findings.mechanism: Every sweep starts a fresh budget and iterates the same SELECT order without a cursor or last-verified ordering. The same early rows consume the budget repeatedly, so some later rows may never have their integrity checked by maintenance.
findings.impact: Background integrity coverage can be permanently incomplete even inside the default 512 MiB store quota. Latent damage in the unvisited portion is not found until it is read or the earlier rows disappear.
findings.fix: Persist or retain a rolling verification cursor, or order by last verification time. Deduplicate shared physical hashes when budgeting work and ensure every retained blob eventually receives a turn.
findings.required_regression_test: Create retained rows totaling more than two scrub budgets, introduce same-size damage in a later row, and run multiple sweeps. Require eventual detection without deleting the earlier rows.
findings.verification: The budget/iteration behavior was exercised in a scaled logic check, not with hundreds of megabytes of media.
findings.qualification: Media reads now verify hashes. This does not resurrect the previous claim that ordinary reads serve same-length corruption unchecked.

findings.title: The password setter is not atomic against the host password command
findings.trigger: The browser setter passes its final stored-hash comparison, then the separate host command resets the password before the browser publishes its replacement.
findings.mechanism: Removing awaits between comparison and write excludes competing JavaScript tasks in one event loop, not another operating-system process. There is no shared lock with the host command. The browser can overwrite the successfully reset host credential and replace its provenance with browser.
findings.impact: Both callers can believe their password change succeeded, but the host reset no longer works. The host-issued terminal enrollment marker can also cease to match the effective credential.
findings.fix: Use a shared inter-process lock and consistent credential/provenance publication protocol in both writers. Revalidate under that lock and define recovery for an interrupted multi-file credential update.
findings.required_regression_test: Run real separate writer processes synchronized after the browser comparison but before its rename. Require one update to reject/retry rather than two successful conflicting publications. Verify credential and provenance consistency.
findings.verification: password-reproductions.mjs executed the SHA-verified SecurityPassword module with real scrypt and filesystem calls. A second Node process performed the host writer publication. Both writes succeeded; only the browser password remained valid.
findings.qualification: Zod and HttpError imports were replaced by narrow valid-input test doubles. This requires an authorized browser change racing an actual host reset; it is not an unauthenticated reset exploit.

findings.title: Reloading the bridge in a live gateway strands the retired sender outbox
findings.trigger: A bridge sender has persisted unsent records, then the plugin is re-registered/reloaded without terminating the hosting gateway process.
findings.mechanism: Registration shuts down the old sender and creates a new incarnation. The old spool still names the same PID and process-start identity as the live gateway. recoverable uses process liveness/identity, not sender incarnation liveness, and therefore treats that retired sender as alive.
findings.impact: Its unsent history can remain excluded from recovery until the gateway process itself exits. The PID-reuse fix correctly distinguishes different processes, but not old and new producers inside one process.
findings.fix: Record sender retirement, use per-incarnation ownership/leases, or explicitly hand old spools to the replacement sender after shutdown. Do not equate a live hosting process with every producer it previously hosted.
findings.required_regression_test: Persist an outbox while offline, call plugin registration again in the same process, restore transport, and require the replacement sender to drain the old incarnation before the host exits.
findings.verification: Source-traced reload and recovery paths. No live Hermes plugin reload was performed.

findings.title: In-flight hold recovery is still outside the shutdown join
findings.trigger: Shutdown overlaps an already running hold-recovery attempt that is awaiting a slow adapter operation.
findings.mechanism: The generic job tracker covers several samplers and sweeps, but recoverHolds is passed directly to retryUntilResolved. That helper discards the active promise; stop only prevents another timer. Hold recovery resumes with database reads and ingestion after adapter awaits, without a shutdown join owned by this helper.
findings.impact: Depending on adapter timing and other shutdown waits, work can resume after dependent resources have begun closing. The general sampler/listener fix does not establish a complete barrier for this path.
findings.fix: Give retryUntilResolved an awaitable close/drain operation or register each invocation in the server job tracker. Stop future admission, await active recovery, and only then close its dependencies.
findings.required_regression_test: Delay port.getTask or taskAction during startup recovery, begin shutdown, and release the delay. Assert no work touches a closed database and no recovery writes occur after the declared shutdown barrier.
findings.verification: Conditional source-level lifecycle analysis. The complete delayed-adapter shutdown scenario was not executed.
findings.qualification: Actual failure depends on adapter cancellation/draining behavior and timing. Keep this distinct from a demonstrated production use-after-close.

findings.title: The new move plan is not durably ordered before filesystem mutation
findings.trigger: Power loss or a storage failure occurs around saving the move plan/progress and publishing the file move or rewrites.
findings.mechanism: savePlan uses writeFile and rename but does not fsync the plan file or its containing directory before the caller proceeds with filesystem mutations. Awaiting those calls establishes completion to the process, not the stronger durability ordering needed for a roll-forward journal.
findings.impact: On affected storage/filesystems, a move or rewrite may survive while its plan/progress does not, weakening the new recovery guarantee. Ordinary process-interruption recovery is a real improvement, but it is a different guarantee from power-loss durability.
findings.fix: Durably publish the plan before any irreversible namespace mutation and durably record progress in the intended order. Fsync the file and parent directory where supported; define and disclose behavior where the platform cannot offer the required guarantee.
findings.required_regression_test: Use a filesystem fault harness or controlled crash/power-loss simulation around plan writes, renames, progress updates, and clearing. Verify that recovery either has enough evidence to converge or reports an explicit recoverable conflict.
findings.verification: Conditional source-level durability analysis. No power-cut or filesystem crash experiment was executed.
findings.qualification: This is not a claim that every process crash loses the plan, nor that rename itself lacks atomic namespace semantics.
